transcript:
This is NPR News Now, the latest headlines every hour.
>> Live from NPR News, I'm Giles Snyder.
Scott Colom is Mississippi's Democratic Senator-elect.
>> For me, this journey started with a prayer, y'all.
And in Mississippi, our prayers have often changed the course of history.
>> Colom speaking to supporters in Jackson.
The Associated Press called his race Wednesday evening more than a week after midterm election day.
Colom narrowly defeated Republican incumbent Senator Cindy Hyde Smith.
Kristin Kaler with Mississippi Public Broadcasting has more.
>> Mail-in and affidavit ballots around the Jackson area have now been counted.
Yvonne Horton, a county election commissioner, says they have one more step before the full process is complete.
>> These numbers, as of right now, are unofficial numbers because we have to come back together as a body, the election commissioner.
Everybody's signature get together and it will be considered official then.
>> Now, the Election Resolution Board will certify all results before it is sent to Mississippi's Secretary of State's office.
For NPR News, I'm Kristin Kaler in Jackson, Mississippi.
>> The White House is warning congressional Democrats not to overreach as they threaten to investigate the Trump administration.
Here's NPR's Tamara Keith.
>> In a letter, White House counsel Will Scharf says the administration is monitoring, quote, "abusive and capricious threats" made by Democrats.
The letter is addressed to Congressman Robert Garcia, who is expected to lead the House Oversight Committee next year and has suggested Trump aides lawyer up.
>> Scharf concludes the administration will not be, quote, "extorted" and will not be cowed by unlawful process motivated by animus, pettiness, or hatred, or any other unlawful motive.
Garcia responded, saying Congress is a co-equal branch of government and will not be deterred by baseless threats.
Tamara Keith, NPR News, the White House.
>> World leaders began their first day of negotiations on Wednesday at the United Nations annual climate summit, urging nations to get tougher on global warming.
NPR's Hadil Al-Shalchari reports from Antalya, Turkey.
>> 197 nations are represented at the two-week conference, also known as COP 31, to discuss how to curb climate change.
UN Secretary General Antonio Guterres made an urgent appeal.
We know the truth, now we must act on it.
Because climate action is more than a fight over a number or a thermometer.
We are in the fight for our lives and our children's future.
>> Scientists say that global warming is set to surpass 1.5 degrees Celsius, or 2.7 Fahrenheit, in a few years, increasing the risk of catastrophic rising of sea level and the collapse of ecosystems.
The U.S. administration was absent from the summit for a second year in a row.
Hadil Al-Shalchari, NPR News, Antalya.
>> And you're listening to NPR News.
President Trump says a triumphal arch he wants to build could also be dedicated to military veterans.
He made the suggestion during his Veterans Day speech at Arlington National Cemetery.
The 250-foot arch would be built nearby, but it's facing legal hurdles.
Three veterans have joined a lawsuit to stop the project, so have multiple members of the Kennedy family.
They argue the arch would obstruct a clear view of the grave site of former President John F. Kennedy and permanently cast a shadow over the graves of servicemen and women.
A federal appeals court panel has ruled that the Justice Department cannot compel the social media platform LinkedIn to hand over vast trolls of correspondence involving journalists simply because it's investigating a national security leak.
The opinion found that violates constitutional protections by interfering with the press.
Here's NPR's David Focumflick.
>> Which journalists are involved?
What secrets were disclosed?
We don't know.
We only know of the case at all because LinkedIn fought the subpoenas of information as overly broad, likely to capture a ton of correspondence between journalists and sources that had nothing to do with the leak.
>> Federal appeals court judge Harvey Wilkinson III wrote that the district court should not have approved prosecutor searches simply because, quote, "The records requested are logistically feasible to compile.
The ruling orders that the search be narrowed."
He also wrote that the First Amendment is first is no mere irrelevance.
He continued, "It captures both who we are as a people and what we aspire to become."
David Focumflick, NPR News.
>> And I'm Giles Snyder.
This is NPR News.

topics.text: Scott Colom wins Mississippi Senate race over Republican incumbent Cindy Hyde Smith
White House warns congressional Democrats against overreach in threatened investigations
UN climate summit in Antalya, Turkey opens with calls for tougher action on warming
Trump suggests triumphal arch near Arlington could also honor military veterans
Federal appeals court limits Justice Department subpoena for LinkedIn records of journalists in leak probe
